The disclosed subject matter relates to a class of (meth)acryloyl compounds represented by formula (A), in which the molecular framework can be selected and modified within defined structural limits to provide compounds having desired reactivity, physical properties, and compatibility with various resin systems. In these compounds, one or more (meth)acryloyl groups are introduced into a molecule through specified linking groups and core structures, thereby producing polymerizable compounds suitable for use in curable compositions, crosslinkable materials, and functional resin formulations.

In formula (A), the central core may be selected from a range of allowable organic structures, including aliphatic, alicyclic, aromatic, heteroatom-containing, or combined structural units. The core may be linear, branched, cyclic, or polycyclic, depending on the intended application and the required balance of rigidity, flexibility, hydrophobicity, polarity, and steric characteristics. The formula further permits a variety of linking groups connecting the core to the (meth)acryloyl moiety. These linkages may include, for example, ester, ether, carbonate, urethane, amide, alkylene, arylene, oxyalkylene, or other divalent connecting groups, provided that they satisfy the structural requirements of the formula. By selecting different linkages, the resulting compound can be designed to exhibit specific curing behavior, adhesion, toughness, transparency, chemical resistance, or thermal performance.

The substituents permitted in formula (A) may also be varied within the defined scope. Such substituents can include hydrogen, alkyl groups, cycloalkyl groups, aryl groups, alkoxy groups, halogen atoms, hydroxyl-containing groups, heteroatom-containing groups, or other functional groups compatible with the (meth)acryloyl structure. The variables in the formula, such as the number of repeating units, the number of polymerizable groups, the length of spacer groups, and the substitution pattern on the core, are each assigned allowable ranges. These ranges enable precise control over molecular weight, functionality, viscosity, curing speed, crosslink density, solubility, and mechanical properties of cured products.

The term “(meth)acryloyl” as used herein encompasses both acryloyl and methacryloyl groups. Accordingly, compounds within the scope of formula (A) may contain acrylate groups, methacrylate groups, or combinations of both. Acrylate-containing compounds may provide high polymerization reactivity and rapid curing, whereas methacrylate-containing compounds may offer improved handling stability, reduced shrinkage, or different mechanical characteristics. The ability to select between these groups further contributes to the broad design flexibility of the disclosed compounds.

Because the structure of the compound can be varied through selection of the core, linkage, substituents, and numerical parameters, the compounds represented by formula (A) provide a versatile platform for molecular design. They can be tailored for use as monomers, oligomeric monomers, reactive diluents, crosslinking agents, resin modifiers, adhesion-promoting components, or intermediates for preparing more complex functional materials. In particular, their polymerizable (meth)acryloyl groups make them useful in radical-curable systems, including ultraviolet-curable, electron-beam-curable, thermally curable, and chemically initiated resin compositions.

The claimed compounds are significant because they combine broad structural tunability with practical polymerization functionality. By adjusting the number and placement of (meth)acryloyl groups, it is possible to control the crosslinking density and network architecture of cured materials. By modifying the core structure and spacer length, it is possible to influence flexibility, hardness, refractive index, heat resistance, water resistance, adhesion to substrates, and compatibility with other resin components. As a result, the compounds may be applied in coatings, adhesives, sealants, inks, photoresists, optical materials, dental materials, 3D-printing resins, composite matrices, electronic materials, and other polymerizable or crosslinkable systems.

Thus, the disclosed class of (meth)acryloyl compounds represented by formula (A) provides a broad and adaptable family of materials. The defined formula establishes the permissible molecular architectures while allowing extensive variation in the core, linkages, substituents, and numerical ranges. This combination of structural definition and design freedom makes the compounds useful both as final functional resin components and as intermediates for preparing advanced polymerizable materials.
outputs.L5:
A (meth)acryloyl compound is a chemical compound that contains an acryloyl group, a methacryloyl group, or both. The term “(meth)acryloyl” is commonly used as shorthand to refer to either acrylate-based or methacrylate-based structures. These compounds are widely used in the production of polymers, coatings, adhesives, sealants, inks, and dental or medical materials.

The key feature of a (meth)acryloyl compound is the presence of a polymerizable carbon–carbon double bond. This double bond allows the compound to undergo radical polymerization, often initiated by heat, light, or chemical initiators. As a result, (meth)acryloyl compounds are especially valuable in UV-curable and electron-beam-curable formulations, where rapid curing and strong film formation are required.

Examples of (meth)acryloyl compounds include acrylic acid derivatives, methacrylic acid derivatives, acrylate esters, methacrylate esters, acrylamides, and methacrylamides. Depending on their molecular structure, these compounds can provide different properties such as hardness, flexibility, adhesion, chemical resistance, transparency, or weatherability. Monofunctional (meth)acryloyl compounds typically improve flexibility and reduce viscosity, while multifunctional compounds can increase crosslinking density, resulting in harder and more durable materials.

In industrial applications, (meth)acryloyl compounds play an important role in high-performance resin systems. They are used to create protective coatings for plastics, metals, wood, and glass, as well as pressure-sensitive adhesives and 3D printing resins. Their ability to cure quickly and form strong polymer networks makes them useful in applications requiring efficiency, durability, and precise control of material properties.

Overall, a (meth)acryloyl compound is an important class of reactive monomers and oligomers in modern polymer chemistry. Its versatility, high reactivity, and ability to form tailored polymer networks make it essential in many advanced material technologies.

In some embodiments, the term “(meth)acryloyl compound” refers to a compound comprising one or more acryloyl and/or methacryloyl groups and represented by the following general formula:

\[
\left[ \mathrm{CH_2=C(R^a)-C(=O)-Z} \right]_n-X-(R^1)_m
\]

wherein \(R^a\) is hydrogen or methyl; \(n\) is an integer of 1 or greater, for example 1 to 10; \(m\) is 0 or an integer of 1 or greater; \(Z\), independently at each occurrence, is oxygen, sulfur, or a direct bond/no linkage; \(X\) is a single bond or a multivalent organic group having 1 to 60 carbon atoms; and each \(R^1\), independently, is selected from alkyl, aryl, alkenyl, alkoxy, halogen, nitro, amino, carboxylic acid, thiol, hydroxy, and hydroxy substituted with a vinylphenylmethyl group.

As used herein, “(meth)acryloyl” includes both acryloyl groups \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-C(=O)-}\) and methacryloyl groups \(\mathrm{CH_2=C(CH_3)-C(=O)-}\). The multivalent organic group \(X\) may be linear, branched, cyclic, aromatic, heteroatom-containing, saturated, or unsaturated, and may optionally contain one or more ether, thioether, ester, amide, urethane, carbonate, siloxane, or aromatic linkages, provided that \(X\) has a valence sufficient to attach to the indicated substituents. The phrase “no linkage” for \(Z\) means that the carbonyl carbon of the (meth)acryloyl group is directly bonded to \(X\).
